rows: Original design
What was built
Why the change was made, and what it cost
Riverpod for state management
provider with ChangeNotifier

I had never written Dart. Riverpod's providers, refs and code generation are three new ideas before the first screen renders. ChangeNotifier is one class with one method. The architecture needs only a view-model that can be constructed in a test, and both give that. Cost: ChangeNotifier rebuilds more widgets than it needs to, which would matter on a longer list than three stations.
Six backend services
Two cloud functions, everything else straight to the database under access rules

Six services was a Milestone 1 estimate made before any were written. Two were enough because only two operations must be out of the client's reach: issuing a code and judging one. The rest are reads a client may safely do. Cost: the access rules now carry logic that would otherwise be in a service, and rules are harder to test than code.
A GPS map of nearby stations
A list of three seeded stations

The map needed the Maps SDK, a billing-enabled API key and runtime location permission. That is the largest block of unfamiliar work in the project and it demonstrates nothing the list does not. Cut deliberately and early, not abandoned.
Separate sign-in and registration screens
One screen with a toggle

The usability target caps a booking at four screens. Spending one of them on a choice the user must make before they have seen a single locker is poor value, because the choice carries no information for them: a first-time user does not yet know they are a first-time user of this system.
Check membership when the user tries to book
Membership decides which screen the app shows at all

A check at booking time is one condition in one place, and any later change to that screen can remove it. Choosing the screen from the account state cannot be removed by accident. The rule became structural rather than checked.
Five two-week sprints
Three one-week sprints
Twenty-three days remained when work started. Two-week sprints would have given one and a half of them, which is not a cadence. Cost: no gap between building something and seeing it again.
Cloud functions deployed
Cloud functions in the local emulator
Deployment requires Google's paid plan and a payment method. The emulator runs the same TypeScript with the same tests. What is untested is the deployment itself.
Each build sent to testers through Firebase App Distribution
Each build tested and gated, none distributed

This was one of the two Rugby elements Milestone 1 took, and only half of it survived. Every push still runs the suite and fails below 70% coverage. Nothing was distributed because there was no second device and no tester to install it, so the delivery half had no recipient. Cost: the review step shows screenshots rather than an installable app, which is what Rugby's continuous delivery exists to avoid.
